caption:
A simple blood test is back in the spotlight.

On November 12 the American Cancer Society revised its prostate cancer screening guidelines. Men at higher risk, meaning Black men and men with a strong family history, should get a PSA blood test every year starting at age 45.

For men at average risk, the group now recommends a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69. Its 2010 guideline left screening to each man's choice after a talk with his doctor. From age 70 it is an individual decision, and screening should stop after 80 or when a man is not expected to live another 10 years.

A PSA level of 3.0 ng/mL or higher is now considered high for men 45 to 69. Many labs in the U.S. report anything under 4.0 as normal. After two elevated readings, the guideline points to an MRI or other biomarker tests before a biopsy, to reduce unnecessary ones. It also stresses active surveillance, so a slow-growing cancer does not automatically mean treatment right away.

The catch: the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force still recommends against routine screening for the whole population. Its advice decides which services insurers must cover, and it has announced an update.

Source: STAT News, American Cancer Society
